headline: The daughter of a jailed president leads Peru

sources.title: Keiko Fujimori sworn in as Peru president after narrow election win
Keiko Fujimori takes office as Peru's president, vowing to end decade of instability

chunks.text: Keiko Fujimori became president of Peru on July 28, at the age of 51 and at her fourth [[attempt]]. She had lost three earlier elections. She won this one by fewer than 50,000 votes in a [[second round]] in June. She now {{takes over}} a country that has {{gone through}} eight presidents in ten years, in a system where governments rarely {{last out}} a full [[term]].

verbs.correct: To use up one after another

chunks.text: Her [[surname]] is the reason many Peruvians voted for her and the reason many others voted against. Her father, Alberto Fujimori, ruled Peru in the 1990s. During those years the state {{put down}} a violent [[rebellion]] and the economy became [[stable]]. Those same years ended with him leaving office in [[disgrace]], and he was later [[sentenced]] to 16 years in prison for [[corruption]] and for [[crimes against humanity]]. [[Supporters]] say he {{brought back}} order to a country close to [[collapse]]. [[Opponents]] say he {{did away with}} democratic limits and that people died because of it. Both of those things are in the record.

verbs.correct: To stop a revolt by force
verbs.wrong: To write a name on a list

chunks.text: Keiko Fujimori has {{taken up}} crime as her main issue, which is what most Peruvians tell [[pollsters]] worries them. She has promised what she calls [[an iron fist]]. That means a very large new prison, more police on the streets, and judges whose names are not published so that criminals cannot [[threaten]] them. Human rights groups have already {{spoken out}} about those [[anonymous]] judges. Their argument is that a [[defendant]] cannot properly {{stand up for}} himself in a court when he does not know who is judging him.

verbs.wrong: To fill an amount of space

chunks.text: Whether she can {{hold on to}} power long enough to do any of it is the open question. Peru's [[Congress]] has {{pushed out}} several recent presidents, and her party does not control it. She has {{called on}} other parties to work alongside her. In a country that has changed leader almost every year, simply reaching the end of a full term would be unusual.
